title: PHARM · Blood transfusion reaction (STOP THE BLOOD, KEEP THE VEIN) (high stakes, night shift, Smart Prep errors)
hook: Nurses: 10 minutes into blood, her back hurts. Slow it?
hook_backups: Nurses: chills during a transfusion. Just slow it down?
Nurses: blood running, fever 38.6. Call first or stop first?
belief: A reaction during a transfusion means you slow the blood and call.

story.patient: 76-year-old woman with a stomach bleed, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, getting her first unit of packed red blood cells

timeline.beat: First unit of blood starts. Patient and nurse in frame with the hook
'Can you do her 15-minute vitals?' The nurse leaves the aide with her
timeline.mistake_line: Left the first 15 minutes to the aide

timeline.beat: 'My back hurts. I'm so cold.' Chills, temp 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), heart rate 118. The nurse slows the blood
timeline.mistake_line: Slowed the blood instead of stopping it

timeline.beat: Pages the provider and waits for a call back. The blood is still running
timeline.mistake_line: Called first, stopped the blood later

timeline.beat: BP (blood pressure) 78/44, dark red urine, oozing at the IV (intravenous) site
timeline.outcome: A transfusion reaction, worse with every minute the blood ran. 3 mistakes. Every one avoidable.

caught_it.text: Two-person check at the bedside: two identifiers, the unit, the order
The RN stays with her for the first 15 minutes, vitals per policy
Back pain, chills, fever: STOP the blood now
Keep the vein open: normal saline with new tubing. Stay, vitals, call the provider and blood bank

choice.question: Blood running. Back pain, chills, fever.
choice.a: Slow it down, call the provider
choice.b: Stop it, saline with new tubing, call

save_card.title: TRANSFUSION REACTION (STOP THE BLOOD, KEEP THE VEIN)
items: First 15 minutes: the RN stays
Back pain, chills, fever: stop the blood
Keep the vein open: saline, new tubing
Call the provider and blood bank, send the bag and tubing back

memory_line: Reaction? Stop the blood, keep the vein.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 1:10 AM. She's 76, a stomach bleed, hemoglobin 6.8. Her first unit of blood starts.

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Scope error: left the first 15 minutes to the aide
2️⃣ Habit over standard: back pain and chills, so the nurse slowed the blood
3️⃣ Wrong priority: paged the provider and waited, blood still running
➡️ 1:45 AM: BP (blood pressure) 78/44, dark red urine. Rapid response.

🩸 Transfusion reaction (STOP THE BLOOD, KEEP THE VEIN)
• Watch closely in the first 15 minutes: the most dangerous reactions often start early
• Signs: back pain, chills, fever, fast heart rate, low BP, dark urine, trouble breathing, hives

✅ The right move
• Two-person check at the bedside before it starts
• The RN (registered nurse) stays for the first 15 minutes, vitals per policy
• Any reaction sign: stop the blood first
• Keep the vein open with normal saline and new tubing
• Stay, vitals, call the provider and the blood bank. Send the bag and tubing back, per policy

🧠 Reaction? Stop the blood, keep the vein.

title: PHARM · Oxygen in COPD (88 TO 92, NEVER ZERO) (high stakes, night shift, Smart Prep errors)
hook: Nurses: COPD, SpO2 82% at 2 AM. Hold the oxygen?
hook_backups: Nurses: oxygen stops a COPD patient breathing. True?
Nurses: his sats are 82. 'That's his normal.' Is it?
belief: Oxygen is dangerous in COPD, so you hold it even when sats are low.

'Oxygen stops his drive to breathe.' The oxygen stays off
He's drowsy. 'Finally sleeping.' No recheck
SpO2 74%, hard to wake, heart rate 132
timeline.outcome: Too little oxygen, not too much. 3 mistakes. Every one avoidable.

caught_it.text: Low oxygen? Give oxygen. Never withhold it
COPD with a CO2 (carbon dioxide) risk: controlled oxygen, target SpO2 88 to 92%
Nasal cannula or a Venturi mask, as ordered or per protocol
Recheck SpO2, breathing, alertness. Drowsy or confused? Call now, blood gas as ordered

choice.question: COPD. SpO2 82%, breathing 28.
choice.a: Hold oxygen to protect his drive

save_card.title: COPD + LOW OXYGEN (88 TO 92, NEVER ZERO)
items: Low oxygen? Never withhold it
Target SpO2 88 to 92% if CO2 risk
Controlled oxygen, as ordered

memory_line: COPD: aim for 88 to 92. Never zero.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 2:15 AM. He's 72 with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), admitted with pneumonia.
• SpO2 (oxygen saturation) 82%, breathing 28, using his neck muscles

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Beyond the stem: "His normal's probably low." No baseline was charted
2️⃣ Habit over standard: held the oxygen for "COPD drive"
3️⃣ Acted too late: called drowsy "sleeping", no recheck
➡️ 3:20 AM: SpO2 74%, hard to wake. Rapid response.

🫁 Oxygen in COPD (88 TO 92, NEVER ZERO)
• Low oxygen kills faster than high CO2 (carbon dioxide)
• Some COPD patients hold on to CO2, so too much oxygen can also make them drowsy
• The answer is controlled oxygen, not none

✅ The right move
• Low oxygen? Give oxygen. Never withhold it
• COPD with a CO2 risk: aim for SpO2 88 to 92%, as ordered
• Nasal cannula or a Venturi mask, as ordered or per protocol
• Recheck SpO2, breathing and alertness. Drowsy or confused? Call now, blood gas as ordered

🧠 COPD: aim for 88 to 92. Never zero.

title: PHARM · IV fluids in heart failure (ASSESS BEFORE YOU POUR) (high stakes, night shift, Smart Prep errors)
hook: Nurses: weak heart, BP 86/50. Open the fluids?
hook_backups: Nurses: low BP at 3 AM. A fluid bolus fixes it?
Nurses: BP 86/50 and she's asleep. Bolus now?
belief: Low blood pressure always means give fluids fast.

story.patient: 79-year-old woman with heart failure (a weak pump), admitted with a urinary infection; she had her evening blood pressure pills

timeline.beat: Automatic cuff: BP (blood pressure) 86/50. She's asleep. Patient and nurse in frame with the hook
'She's dry.' The IV (intravenous) saline goes wide open, 1 liter. Nobody listens to her lungs
timeline.mistake_line: Treated a number before assessing her

timeline.beat: No call, no order for the bolus
timeline.mistake_line: Gave a fluid bolus with no order

timeline.beat: Crackles, a wet cough, 'I can't lie flat.' 'Just a cold.' Fluids keep running
timeline.mistake_line: Heard crackles, kept the fluids running

timeline.beat: SpO2 (oxygen saturation) 84%, breathing 32, pink frothy sputum
timeline.outcome: Fluid in her lungs. 3 mistakes. Every one avoidable.

caught_it.text: Recheck the BP by hand. Look at her: alert? dizzy?
Listen to her lungs, check swelling and urine, review tonight's BP pills
Call the provider with your findings. Fluids only as ordered, then reassess
Crackles or breathless on fluids: stop them, sit her up, oxygen, call

choice.question: Heart failure. BP 86/50, asleep, no complaints.

save_card.title: HEART FAILURE + LOW BP (ASSESS BEFORE YOU POUR)
items: Recheck the BP by hand
Lungs, swelling, urine, tonight's meds
Fluids only as ordered, then reassess
Crackles or breathless: stop, sit up, call

memory_line: Weak pump, low BP: assess before you pour.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 3:05 AM. She's 79 with heart failure (a weak pump). She had her evening blood pressure pills.
• BP (blood pressure) 86/50 on the automatic cuff. Asleep

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Acted too soon: opened 1 liter of saline wide, never assessed her
2️⃣ Scope error: gave a fluid bolus with no order
3️⃣ Acted too late: crackles and a wet cough called "just a cold", fluids kept running
➡️ 4:10 AM: SpO2 (oxygen saturation) 84%, pink frothy sputum. Rapid response.

💧 IV (intravenous) fluids in heart failure (ASSESS BEFORE YOU POUR)
• A weak pump can't move extra fluid forward
• It backs up into the lungs: crackles, a wet cough, breathless lying flat
• A low BP has many causes. Find hers first

✅ The right move
• Recheck the BP by hand and look at her
• Listen to the lungs, check swelling and urine, review tonight's meds
• Call the provider. Fluids only as ordered, then reassess
• Crackles or breathless on fluids: stop them, sit her up, oxygen, call

🧠 Weak pump, low BP: assess before you pour.

title: PHARM · Hydralazine vs hydroxyzine (READ EVERY LETTER) (high stakes, night shift, Smart Prep errors)
hook: Nurses: hydrALAZINE or hydrOXYzine? One letter. One crash.
hook_backups: Nurses: the scanner beeps 'wrong drug' at 2 AM. Override?
Nurses: he asked for an anxiety pill. Why did his BP crash?
belief: Drugs that start the same are close enough to grab fast.

story.patient: 81-year-old man who can't sleep and feels anxious; as-needed order: hydrOXYzine 25 mg by mouth for anxiety

timeline.beat: 'I'm so anxious, I can't sleep.' Patient and nurse in frame with the hook
Two bins side by side. The nurse reads 'hydr...' and grabs hydrALAZINE 25 mg
The scanner beeps 'wrong drug'. 'It's acting up.' Override
'I feel dizzy.' The nurse finishes the med pass first
timeline.mistake_line: Finished the med pass before the dizzy patient

timeline.beat: BP (blood pressure) 84/48, heart rate 112, dizzy and confused
timeline.outcome: One letter. 3 mistakes. Every one avoidable.

caught_it.text: Read the whole name. Tall-man letters: hydrALAZINE, hydrOXYzine
Scan every dose. A scanner alert means stop and check
Match the drug to the reason: anxiety is hydroxyzine, blood pressure is hydralazine
Dizzy after a dose? Him first: BP, stay with him, call

choice.question: 2 AM. The scanner says 'wrong drug'.
choice.b: Stop, read every letter, check the order

save_card.title: HYDRALAZINE VS HYDROXYZINE (READ EVERY LETTER)
items: hydrALAZINE: lowers blood pressure
hydrOXYzine: eases anxiety and itching
Scanner alert: stop and check
Dizzy after a dose: BP first, then call

memory_line: One letter apart. Read every letter.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 2:30 AM. He's 81, anxious, can't sleep. His as-needed order: hydrOXYzine 25 mg by mouth.

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Missed keyword: read "hydr..." and grabbed hydrALAZINE
2️⃣ Habit over standard: the scanner said "wrong drug", and the nurse overrode it
3️⃣ Wrong priority: "I feel dizzy", and the med pass came first
➡️ 3:45 AM: BP (blood pressure) 84/48, dizzy and confused. Rapid response.

🔤 Hydralazine vs hydroxyzine (READ EVERY LETTER)
• hydrALAZINE: relaxes the arteries and lowers blood pressure
• hydrOXYzine: an antihistamine for anxiety and itching
• Look-alike, sound-alike names: tall-man letters show the difference

✅ The right move
• Read the whole name, every letter
• Scan every dose. A scanner alert means stop and check
• Match the drug to the reason it's ordered
• Dizzy after a dose? Check BP, stay with him, call

🧠 One letter apart. Read every letter.

title: PHARM · Bupropion XL: do not crush (XL MEANS WHOLE) (high stakes, night shift, Smart Prep errors)
hook: Nurses: she can't swallow pills. Crush the XL?
hook_backups: Nurses: crushed into applesauce at 5 AM. Then a seizure.
Nurses: two letters on the label decide everything. Which?
belief: Any pill can be crushed if the patient can't swallow it.

story.patient: 73-year-old woman with trouble swallowing since a stroke last year; bupropion XL (extended release) 300 mg every morning for depression

timeline.beat: Early med pass. 'I can't swallow big pills.' Patient and nurse in frame with the hook
Every pill crushed into applesauce. Nobody reads 'XL' on the label
'Can you give her this?' The cup goes to the nursing assistant
timeline.mistake_line: Asked the aide to give the meds

timeline.beat: Jittery, twitching, heart rate 116. 'Just anxious.'
A seizure
timeline.outcome: The whole day's dose, all at once. 3 mistakes. Every one avoidable.

caught_it.text: XL, ER, SR, CR, LA on the label: never crush. A few can be split or opened: ask pharmacy
Can't swallow it whole? Hold it, call pharmacy and the provider for another form
In the hospital, the nurse gives the meds
New twitching or jitters after a dose: check her, seizure precautions, report

choice.question: Bupropion XL due. She can't swallow tablets.
choice.b: Hold it, call pharmacy for another form

save_card.title: DO NOT CRUSH (XL MEANS WHOLE)
items: XL, ER, SR, CR, LA: never crush
Crushed XL: the whole dose at once
Can't swallow? Ask pharmacy for another form
Bupropion too fast: seizure risk

caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 5:20 AM med pass. She's 73, trouble swallowing since a stroke. Bupropion XL (extended release) 300 mg every morning.

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Missed keyword: crushed every pill, never read "XL"
2️⃣ Scope error: handed the cup to the nursing assistant to give
3️⃣ Acted too late: twitching and jitters called "just anxious"
➡️ 6:30 AM: a seizure. Rapid response.

💊 Bupropion XL (XL MEANS WHOLE)
• XL tablets release the dose slowly over the day
• Crushed, the whole day's dose hits at once
• Bupropion's seizure risk climbs with dose and speed

✅ The right move
• XL, ER (extended release), SR (sustained release), CR (controlled release), LA (long acting) on the label: never crush. A few can be split or opened: ask pharmacy
• Can't swallow it? Hold it and call pharmacy and the provider for another form
• In the hospital, the nurse gives the meds
• New twitching or jitters: check her, seizure precautions, report

🧠 XL means whole. Never crush.

title: PHARM · Promethazine IV (NEVER PUSH IT) (high stakes, night shift, Smart Prep errors)
hook: Nurses: 2 AM nausea. Push promethazine in her hand IV?
hook_backups: Nurses: 'It burns!' Keep pushing the promethazine?
Nurses: one quick IV push. Her hand turns white by morning.
belief: Promethazine is a routine quick IV push for nausea.

story.patient: 68-year-old woman after gallbladder surgery, nauseated; order: promethazine 12.5 mg IV (intravenous) every 6 hours as needed. Her only IV is in the back of her hand

timeline.beat: 'I'm going to be sick.' Patient and nurse in frame with the hook
Pushes it straight from the vial, undiluted, in under a minute
timeline.mistake_line: Pushed it undiluted: the label changed in 2023

timeline.beat: Into the hand IV. The label says never a hand or wrist vein
timeline.mistake_line: Skipped 'never in the hand or wrist'

timeline.beat: 'It burns!' The nurse keeps pushing
Her hand is pale, cold and swollen, the fingers dusky, blisters forming
timeline.outcome: A badly injured hand from one push. 3 mistakes. Every one avoidable.

caught_it.text: Preferred route: deep IM (intramuscular)
IV only if needed: dilute in normal saline (1 mg/mL max), infuse over 20 to 40 minutes
A large vein, ideally central. Never the hand or wrist
Burning or pain: stop now and report

choice.question: Promethazine IV ordered. Her only IV is in her hand.
choice.a: Push it: it's a small dose
choice.b: Ask for IM or a large vein, dilute, infuse

save_card.title: PROMETHAZINE IV (NEVER PUSH IT)
items: Preferred: deep IM (into the muscle)
IV: dilute (1 mg/mL max), infuse over 20 to 40 min
Large vein. Never the hand or wrist
Burning or pain: stop and report

memory_line: Promethazine: dilute, drip, big vein. Never push.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 2:10 AM. She's 68, nauseated after gallbladder surgery. Promethazine 12.5 mg IV (intravenous) as needed. Her only IV is in her hand.

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Knowledge gap: pushed it undiluted. The label changed in 2023
2️⃣ Missed keyword: into a hand vein, which the label rules out
3️⃣ Acted too late: "It burns!" and the nurse kept pushing
➡️ 6:30 AM: her hand pale, cold, fingers dusky. Urgent surgery consult.

💉 Promethazine IV (NEVER PUSH IT)
• It can damage tissue badly if it leaks from the vein or enters an artery
• Injuries have included gangrene and amputation
• Deep IM (intramuscular) is the preferred route

✅ The right move
• Ask whether IM, or another antiemetic, is an option
• IV only if needed: dilute in normal saline (1 mg/mL or less) and infuse over 20 to 40 minutes, per the label
• A large vein, ideally central. Never the hand or wrist
• Burning or pain: stop now and report

🧠 Promethazine: dilute, drip, big vein. Never push.
